transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 09:42 PT
Duration: 52m (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam Park (Redwood CSM - 10m), Asha Patel (Head of ML, Silvergate), Ben Lowe (Platform Eng), Nina Romero (CTO)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Silvergate is exploring cost and hosting tradeoffs for powering a document-understanding + agent layer used in their deal flow product. They have a constrained monthly budget for inference and want to understand per-token economics, batching + KV/prefix cache levers, and whether Dedicated capacity or Hosted with routing/fallbacks is the best path. Action items and a pilot were agreed.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching strategies, prefix/KV cache, dedicated vs hosted capacity, latency SLO, pilot scope, security requirements (KMS/SSO/SOC2).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): ok everyone good morning, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros — I'll run through what we usually do on econ discovery calls and then Diego can deep dive on the batching/cache levers.
[00:12] Asha (Silvergate): hi, thanks. I'm Asha, head of ML here. We run model-based document ingestion and a conversational layer for deal teams. We care a lot about latency for interactive queries and cost per month — we have a hard cap for pilot.
[00:25] Ben (Silvergate): Ben here, platform. We'll own the pilot infra and security side. Short ask: we need an apples-to-apples cost model across hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:34] Diego (Redwood SE): great. quick high level: Redwood hosted charges per-token on generation and embeddings, but the unit economics change a lot with batching and cache hit-rate. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — monthly commit, better throughput predictability and lower per-token run when you amortize. Private adds networking/security overhead.
[00:52] Nina (CTO): timeline — we want to decide by end of July for a Q3 pilot. Budget: pilot has a $15k/month cap unless we justify spend.
[01:06] Maya: perfect. let's map those constraints. First, traffic profile — are you mostly short interactive prompts or long document generations?
[01:16] Asha: mix. 70% short Q/A (average 80 tokens output), 20% reranking/embeddings, 10% long summarization (avg 700 tokens). Average concurrency maybe 30 qps during peak. We can share a histogram.
[01:31] Ben: and residency — data mustn't leave our VPC for production; pilot can use hosted if there's a secure tunnel and audit logs. SOC2 is required and SSO (SAML).
[01:44] Diego: noted. For cost modeling, two levers really change things: batching (we can batch up to N requests into one forward pass) and KV/prefix cache (for repeated context or assistant style prompts). We typically model three scenarios: conservative (no batching), opportunistic batching, and aggressive batching with KV cache.
[02:05] Maya: I'll hand over to Diego for numbers — Diego, show them a rough example.
[02:09] Diego: OK, example: assume a 13B open model equivalent. Per-token baseline on hosted unbatched is X (he mumbles numbers) — sorry numbers vary by model; I'll give normalized numbers in the spreadsheet. But imagine unbatched per-token cost of 0.004 cents, batching reduces that to 0.0015 cents at effective batch 8, and with 60% cache hit-rates you could drop effective tokens billed by model by another 30-40% depending on prefix lengths.
[02:44] Asha: cache hit-rate — is that per-session prefix or per-customer shared cache? We have a mix of similar system prompts and repeated documents.
[02:52] Diego: both. prefix caching helps when the system prompt or large retrieved context repeats across requests; KV cache is more about key-value attention caching for incremental generation to avoid re-computation. For retrieval-augmented flows, caching retrieved chunks can avoid repeated tokenization and rerun.
[03:12] Ben: for the pilot we care about two numbers: 1) per-interaction incremental cost and 2) peak provisioned throughput with acceptable p95 latency under 800ms. If dedicated reduces cost but increases latency predictability, that's a trade we need quantified.
[03:29] Diego: dedicated gives you reserved slots — the amortized GPU cost goes down because you're not paying per-token egress markup. You get lower tail-latency variance. Hosted gives easier ramp and lower upfront. Private (on-prem) is the highest up-front ops but can be cost-effective at very high scale.
[03:48] Maya: also consider fallback policies — you can route burst traffic to a cheaper model or to a hosted fall-back to avoid dropped requests. That's a lever to control budget overages.
[03:58] Nina: question: how do you calculate effective per-token when you have streaming? Our UI streams partial answers.
[04:05] Diego: streaming doesn't change billing — billed tokens are the same, but streaming impacts early-latency perceptions. For billing we use generated tokens; if you can truncate early or set stop tokens that's a knob. Also aggressive early-stopping hyperparams cut average output length.
[04:21] Asha: any sample numbers for an 80-token average interactive prompt at 30 qps peak?
[04:29] Diego: rough back-of-envelope: with opportunistic batching (batched to effective 4) and 20% cache hits, cost per interaction might be ~0.5 to 0.7 cents. Unbatched could be 2-3x that. But I'll attach a spreadsheet with model-specific rows — these rough gaps just show why batching matters.
[04:49] Ben: can you explain the dedicated pricing model? We prefer predictable monthly rather than per-token variability.
[04:56] Maya: Dedicated is a monthly reserved capacity commitment for a GPU pool. You pick a capacity tier e.g. N concurrent slots or N GPUs. There's a base fee and a reduced per-token execution charge. You also get options for burst capacity. We can map pilot sizes to a small reserved pool for the pilot window so it fits your $15k/month cap.
[05:14] Diego: note that dedicated still benefits from batching/caching — those savings compound. Also quantization options (8-bit/4-bit) change throughput and cost. We'll recommend specific model+quantization combos based on quality targets.
[05:28] Asha: how about cold-starts and KV cache warmup? If we route across regions or models, does cache land on the machine?
[05:36] Diego: caches are per-instance; warmup matters. For Dedicated we can pre-warm with a representative set. For Hosted we have global caches and prefix caching can be sticky per-tenant. If the pilot uses a small set of repeated documents, expect high effective hit rates quickly.
[05:52] Nina: security — can we bring our KMS? We need key control for any document content at rest and in transit.
[05:59] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM integrations. For Hosted we support customer-managed keys for certain enterprise tiers and bring-your-own-key through our KMS integrations; otherwise Redwood-managed keys are default. We'll follow up with the security brief.
[06:14] Ben: latency numbers: what's typical p95 on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[06:20] Diego: p95 depends on model size and batch size. Example: 13B quantized on Dedicated with batch=4 might have p95 ~ 300-450ms for 80-token outputs; Hosted shared noisy neighbors could push p95 higher but we apply isolation and QoS. We'll provide a matrix in the spreadsheet with realistic p50/p95 estimates.
[06:42] Asha: about batching — our app is real-time, can we buffer to create batches without harming UX?
[06:49] Diego: you can use adaptive batching — small time window (10-40ms) to collect requests, or request grouping by route; often for 30 qps you see enough natural coalescing. We also support priority lanes for low-latency traffic that bypass batching if you want guaranteed <200ms.
[07:06] Maya: quick interjection — customers often implement two tiers: interactive lane (low batch, higher cost) and background lane (high batch, lower cost) for non-critical stuff.
[07:18] Ben: if we setup two lanes, can we route automatically based on budget thresholds?
[07:23] Diego: yes — Redwood routing supports budget-based fallbacks and can switch traffic to cheaper model variants or throttle non-essential lanes when spend approaches cap. It's policy driven.
[07:36] Asha: pilot scope question: what would you measure to show it's within our $15k cap?
[07:44] Maya: we'd instrument per-route cost breakdown, p95 latency, cache hit-rate, and token distribution (prompt vs generation) over a weekly window. Diego will create a projection for your traffic profile and show sensitivity to batching and cache hit rates.
[07:59] Ben: operational question — if we go Dedicated for production, can we start Hosted for pilot and then move capacity over keeping the same API surface?
[08:08] Maya: yes, that's a key Redwood promise — same API and routing policies across hosted/dedicated/private. You can pin model versions and route policy changes without code rewrites.
[08:18] Nina: any hidden costs we should budget for? Networking egress? Audit log retention?
[08:24] Diego: good call-outs. Private will have infra costs and possibly higher setup. For hosted, long-term log retention and high-fidelity tracing are add-ons. Egress is typically included, but cross-region replication or dedicated networking tunnels might carry extra charges — we'll call those out in the proposal.
[08:41] Asha: curious about quantization — do you recommend 4-bit for quality-critical summarization?
[08:47] Diego: 4-bit can be close but depends on model. For high-fidelity summarization we often recommend 8-bit with careful calibration, and run evals. We'll include a quality delta table in the deliverable.
[08:59] Maya: ok, let's re-cap action items (quick).
[09:02] Asha: go ahead.
[09:04] Maya: Asha to share sample prompts + traffic histogram; Diego to send cost projection spreadsheet covering hosted/dedicated/private with batching scenarios; Maya to send security brief and pilot contract. We'll schedule a 30m pilot kickoff next week pending docs.
[09:20] Ben: can you also include a simple Dashboard screenshot so our procurement folks see per-route costs?
[09:25] Liam (CSM): yes I can attach a Redwood Console screenshot of per-route cost and token breakdown.
[09:30] Nina: one last Q — if our usage spikes beyond committed Dedicated capacity how do burst and fallback work?
[09:36] Diego: we have a burst pool option and automatic fallback to hosted variants; policies can cap spend and reroute non-critical lanes. We will configure alerting and budget guards so procurement isn't surprised.
[09:48] Asha: good. I'm comfortable moving to pilot if Diego's projection shows we can keep under $15k with realistic hits and some buffer.
[09:55] Maya: great. We'll aim to get the projection and security docs out by Friday. Anything else?
[10:01] Ben: no, thanks all.
[10:03] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with items and a calendared pilot kickoff.

End of transcript.

References shared in call: cost-projection-spreadsheet.xlsx (will be attached by Diego), Redwood security brief link (to be sent), Redwood Console sample screenshot (attached by Liam).

Call wrap/recap (auto): Pilot step agreed contingent on sample prompt data and cost spreadsheet showing feasibility within $15k pilot cap. Next meeting: pilot kickoff (30m) proposed 2026-06-29.
